This is really cool, sorely missed. Is there a way (maybe using `.d.ts` files?) to avoid the repetitive boilerplate typing of Page and Layout components? I.e. instead of:

```ts
export default function DashboardLayout(props: LayoutProps<'/dashboard'>) {
```

…you could do this, and `props` is automatically typed based on the file path:

```ts
export default function DashboardLayout(props) {
```

Don't know if it's possible but I kind of expected it to work like that and was very surprised I had to type them manually.
author: rijk

body: I don’t think it’s possible to get editor type inference / etc. for that case, however at build time Next will cause type _errors_ if you specify a type for `props` that’s _wrong_. But it won’t show inline in the page file, it comes from next.js internals
author: controversial

@rijk unfortunately, @controversial is right. I've spent a few dozen hours trying to find a way to "magically" annotate the page types from outside, but I haven't found a way that actually works with editor type inference (although you can get it to fail `tsc` compilation at build time).

If anyone comes up with some way to make the behavior described work, I'd love to implement it. In the meantime I think this is the best option.

body:
> What's the plan with a dedicated script to generate these? Otherwise you can no longer typecheck your app without `next build` which is way too slow.

@eps1lon I intentionally designed the route generation code to be fairly implementation agnostic, so I can easily make a new `next typegen` command which just traverses the current trajectory and calls into it (this would also resolve your comment on #81528). I thought I would make this as a new PR because though it's a nice feature, it's not necessary for the implementation.

On the other hand, I'm not entirely sure something like this is needed:
- Most people develop while running `next dev`, in which case types are auto-generated instantly and kept up to date.
- In CI, type-generation and type-checking run as part of `next build` anyways

If we do want to add this feature, we could also think about adding it as a sub-component of `npx typecheck` or something similar, which could both generate types and run type-checking. Then we could add a `--watch` flag to that command, automatically run it during `next dev`, and pipe outputs to the user's stdout there (as suggested by @huozhi, and useful for #81400).

> can easily make a new `next typegen` command

I would appreciate this a lot to be able to run in turborepo as a dependency of type checking and typed linting 

Right now we have `eslint.ignoreDuringBuilds` in our `next.config.js` because it takes a very time—instead we parallelize linting with the second half of the build, using turborepo:
1. `next build --experimental-build-mode compile` runs first, to generate the route types
2. in parallel: `eslint` and `next build --experimental-build-mode generate` run

we can’t run eslint before `next build --experimental-build-mode compile` because typed linting depends on the types generated by typedRoutes.

If there were a (fast) `next typegen` command, we could start linting earlier in the build and achieve better parallelization

Agree it wouldn’t need to be blocking for the initial implementation here, but a `next typegen` entry point would be useful for us!
author: controversial

body: Nobody runs `next build` in their CI. That's a big ask just to get typechecking to work. And using typechecking during deploy is annoying for previews where you don't want to block a preview because a type issue. Typechecking during build also problematic if you're resource constrained.
author: eps1lon

body: totally - having the freedom to do typechecking separate from build is huge for dx

body:
> **Not a blocker, just a question:** Is this actually able to catch every possible case of a circular dependency, or only ones where the aggregation parent encounters itself directly as a child? I assume catching arbitrary cycles would be too expensive.

Yeah I also wondered about that. I'm not super sure. Initially I thought no, but I tend to yes now.

Here is my reasoning. We you connect two leaf tasks, the parent ends up increasing the aggregation number of the child to something slightly higher than its own aggregation number. If you do a cycle, I guess they end up doing this in a cycle, so it quickly makes one of the tasks an aggregating task which triggered the panic.

> **Maybe a blocker:** I worry a bit about if it's possible to have a cycle that briefly appears due to eventual consistency that disappears once strongly resolved:
> 
> ```
> a - depends -> b
> b - depends -> c
> ```
> 
> Let's say that `c` is invalidated. As a result of that invalidation, `c` now depends on `a`, forming a cycle.
> 
> `c` returns a different value which invalidates `b`. `b` returns a different value which invalidates `a`. `a` recomputes and now no longer depends on `b` or `c` (e.g. because it's non-deterministic), breaking the cycle.
> 
> If it's not possible to handle for this correctly, some amount of optional cycle detection still seems useful, so maybe we could put this behind an environment variable for debugging?

That case would trigger the panic. Not sure how it behaves without the panic, it causes loops in the aggregated graph, so maybe this will cause "hanging" currently anyway. I'll add a test case.

> can you add a test for a task cycle?

I'll make sure to improve the panic message and add a test case

body:
Yeah, that's also a doable approach. I think I would prefer the macro approach tho.
The generic code ends up being simpler (no double impl Fn(), better compile time) and it actually ends up being dead code that is removed by the Compiler (less binary size, better compile time). The downside is the macros everywhere, but that seems acceptable to me.

I think the _ var names can be removed now. I wrapped the original code in a `if false` block to make the Compiler check it.
author: sokra

body:
@sokra this is subjective, and I respect your opinion, but on a couple points:

> actually ends up being dead code that is removed ... less binary size

the non-macro approach should allow DCE too, it's just not as easy to assert that it actually happens, and it may only happen with higher opt levels.

**EDIT:** It's not exactly 1:1, as I swapped out the underlying event implementation for a dummy `Condvar` (IDK how to add a cargo dependency to godbolt), but I tried modeling this out, and it looks like the unused closure in the non-macro version is completely eliminated even with opt-level=0: https://godbolt.org/z/3hcj9hWK5 -- as far as I can tell it gets eliminated in the Rust frontend, after the MIR, but before the LLVM IR is generated.

> better compile time

I don't think that compilation performance is a concern here either way here as there aren't a ton of callsites, but...

I'm suspect at the assertion that the macros would be faster to compile, as everything I've heard about macros (including declarative macros, though proc macros are way worse) is that they're pretty bad for compilation performance.

Yes, it would likely eliminate the inner expression sooner, but in general, monomorphization should be a little less bad than macro expansion as it happens much later after parsing, typechecking, and borrow checking is complete. It should only create duplicate work for the codegen steps.

body:
Hey @Anas-github-acc. We've been porting some of these scripts to typescript with ESM modules, under the assumption that future Next.js versions will be able to work well with that.

In the meantime, we've been using `tsx` to run similar scripts: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/scripts/pack-next.ts#L1 (see the comment at the top)

I don't want to accept a PR that adds back legacy CJS versions of this stuff, but I'd be willing to accept PRs fixing bugs in these scripts or porting them to TS and/or ESM.

FWIW, I only use the `pack-next` script instead without the `--tar` argument for my work in Turbopack.

body:
The UX of persisting the panel location is really bad

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3d15c88e-d60c-4d07-aedd-dea3bc26e1dc

I don't think we can ship panel location persistence. Though, the alternative- your panel drag location drag resetting every time you close it- will be worse for power users when we have more devtools you will actually debug with! I don't like this solution, the entry point to how you use a devtool is very very important (again, it's not that important yet, but it will be). Open to thoughts here @ztanner @huozhi 

A solution i can think of is making the next logo "part of the panel" when it opens, and not having 2 potential things u can drag at any point on the screen (currently logo and panel)... feels like we're going in circles. I think the problem modeling after the vercel toolbar is that it's not a toolbar optimized for debugging WITH the website, it's more of a raycast like devtool
author: RobPruzan

body: @ztanner already spoke to @huozhi , hold off on reviewing will be splitting this up a bit, and need to push a few cleanups
author: RobPruzan

body:
@huozhi I decided to not split up the PR and instead:
- split into 2 commits (delete old panel stuff, implement new panel)
- decouple changes from old UI. There should be 0 changes to old UI other than minor abstractions to share some logic

the 2nd commit is a bit big, but I think it's pretty linear/easy to review as one big chunk vs split any further. Maybe I would recommend opening `dev-overlay.tsx` in your editor and exploring the `process.env.__NEXT_DEVTOOL_NEW_PANEL_UI` path to its leaves vs using the github UI for a better reviewing experience

body:
Woah, this is wild. I've got a few more ideas if you're willing to try them:

- Join all the `babelIncludeRegexes` into a single regex by concatenating them with `|` operators. This is probably the most expensive check here.
- Move the `node_modules` check to the top. That's the cheapest check and is probably the most likely to be false. I don't think this can be merged with `babelIncludeRegexes`?
- Convert `finalTranspilePackages` into a `Set` (maybe not needed here as it looks like by default it has only one element) and make it the last check (since there's only one thing in there by default, so it's least likely to short-circuit the conditional).

If we do those basic optimizations, I wonder if caching is still worth it or not.
author: bgw

body: @bgw Based on my investigation, the cache is necessary. The key bottleneck is the `isResourceInPackages` function. When I tested joining all `babelIncludeRegexes`, no significant improvement was observed. Note that JavaScript's `Array.some()` method already implements short-circuit evaluation by design. Moving the `node_modules` check to the top of the logic chain theoretically improves performance, which is why I've made this change.

body:
I just went through and polished these changes. A few differences since the last version:
- Squashed commits
- We now generate a separate `.next/types/link.d.ts` file (since `routes.d.ts` contains an `export type` statement, which causes TS to not treat it strictly as an ambient type declaration file, so type augmenting was breaking)
- Switched over to mirror @shuding's original parsing of path-to-regexp strings. This brings more reliability + keeps behavior the same as the previous `experimental.typedRoutes` implementation, at the cost of optional parameters like `:slug?` not working anymore (which imo is a good thing since we don't have optional dynamic single segments in Next.js anyways).

@kevva We're looking at landing this as a part of Next.js 16. These features are currently in experimental and subject to rapid change as a result, I wouldn't recommend using these features in production until we've stabilized the features.
author: wyattjoh

body:
> @kevva We're looking at landing this as a part of Next.js 16. These features are currently in experimental and subject to rapid change as a result, I wouldn't recommend using these features in production until we've stabilized the features.

Yeah gotcha. We've been running Next.js canary with a lot of experimental features without too many issues. body:
**Context** - Next.js 14 App Router - Error during hydration: ``` Hydration failed because the initial UI does not match what was rendered on the server ``` - Happens only in production build **Why** Hydration mismatches mean the HTML generated on the server differs from the first client render. Common causes: - Using `Math.random()`, `Date.now()`, `crypto.randomUUID()` directly in components - Conditionals that depend on `window` / browser APIs (not available at SSR) - Rendering that depends on non-deterministic data (locale, timezone, etc.) - Mismatched markup/attributes between server and client **Fix (minimum viable)** 1) **Remove non-deterministic values from SSR output** - Wrap random/time-based code with `useEffect` or mark as client-only. ```tsx "use client" import { useState, useEffect } from 'react' export default function Example() { const [uuid, setUuid] = useState(null) useEffect(() => setUuid(crypto.randomUUID()), []) return

{uuid ?? 'loading…'}

} ``` 2) **Guard browser-only code** ```tsx "use client" import { useEffect, useState } from 'react' export default function WindowWidth() { const [w, setW] = useState(null) useEffect(() => setW(window.innerWidth), []) return {w ?? 0} } ``` 3) **Check conditionals** - Ensure server and client render the same tree until hydration completes. - If you must branch, render a placeholder until client decides. 4) **Validate build** ```bash rm -rf .next npm run build npm run start ``` Sometimes stale caches hide the mismatch. **Docs** - Hydration error message: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/react-hydration-error - Client components: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/rendering/composition-patterns#client-components If this helps, please **Mark as answer** so others can find it.

> Odd, same error locally. But can't seem to find any references to R in that chunk

@huozhi @Netail 

Hi, we've introduced some code style refactors in the repo after v5.98.0 (i.e. change import path of `runtime.js` - `*.runtime.js` => `*.runtime`), which make those `runtime.js` modules are bundled and minified, then led to the `R is not defined` issue. Could you try resolving it by making the following change in `packages/next/taskfile.js` and then updating the Webpack bundle?

```diff
customEmit(path) {
-  if (path.endsWith('.runtime.js')) return `'./${basename(path)}'`
+  if (/HotModuleReplacement\.runtime|JavascriptHotModuleReplacement\.runtime/.test(path)) 
+    return `'./${basename(path)}'`
},
```

If you have a better solution to address this, feel free to implement it instead. Let me know if you need more details or clarification.
